name: Butter Chicken
description: Chicken cooked in a spiced tomato gravy rich with butter, also called murgh makhani. It was created by chefs Kundan Lal Gujral and Kundan Lal Jaggi and popularised in the 1950s at their Moti Mahal restaurant in Daryaganj, and it has become a staple of the city.
how_to_eat: Scoop it up with butter naan or eat it over rice.
how_to_order: Ask for butter chicken (murgh makhani), half or full, at any Punjabi or Mughlai restaurant.

name: Chole Bhature
description: Spicy chickpea curry with bhature, puffed deep-fried bread leavened with yogurt. Its origins are debated, but it spread to Delhi after Partition and is one of the city's best-loved breakfasts and street foods.
how_to_eat: Tear the bhatura and scoop up the chole, with pickle, onion and chutney on the side.
how_to_order: Ask for a plate of chole bhature in the morning at roadside stalls and old shops such as those in Paharganj.

name: Nihari
description: A stew of slow-cooked meat shanks and bone marrow, cooked overnight and flavoured with long pepper; Delhi is one of the cities credited with its origin. In Old Delhi it is a breakfast dish, with nalli (marrow-bone) nihari especially popular around Jama Masjid.
how_to_eat: Eat it hot, dipping khameeri roti or sheermal into the gravy.
how_to_order: Ask for mutton or nalli nihari early in the morning at eateries near Jama Masjid.

name: Paranthe Wali Gali Paratha
description: Parathas deep-fried in ghee and stuffed with potato, paneer, cauliflower, mixed vegetables, dry fruit, rabri or khoya. They are the speciality of Paranthe Wali Gali, a historic lane off Chandni Chowk.
how_to_eat: Eat it hot with the potato curry, pumpkin sabzi, pickles and chutneys served alongside.
how_to_order: Pick a filling from the board at any shop in Paranthe Wali Gali; parathas are sold by the piece.

name: Chole Kulche
description: Spicy chickpeas served with soft kulcha bread, topped with onion, coriander and tangy seasonings. It is a cheap and filling Delhi street meal.
how_to_eat: Tear the kulcha and eat it with the chole.
how_to_order: Ask for chole kulche at street carts across the city; it is sold by the plate.

name: Dahi Bhalla
description: Soft lentil dumplings soaked in yogurt, topped with tamarind and green chutneys, roasted spices and pomegranate seeds. It is a classic Old Delhi chaat.
how_to_eat: Eat it chilled with a spoon.
how_to_order: Ask for dahi bhalla at chaat stalls in Chandni Chowk.

name: Papri Chaat
description: Crisp fried papri wafers topped with potato, chickpeas, yogurt and sweet and green chutneys. It is one of the signature chaats of Chandni Chowk's chaat sellers.
how_to_eat: Eat it quickly with a spoon before the papri goes soft.
how_to_order: Ask for papri chaat at chaat stalls in Chandni Chowk.

name: Khasta Kachori
description: Flaky deep-fried pastry of refined flour stuffed with spiced moong dal. It is a popular Old Delhi snack, sold from shops near Chandni Chowk.
how_to_eat: Eat it hot, with the potato sabzi or chutneys served alongside.
how_to_order: Ask for khasta kachori by the plate at kachori shops around Chandni Chowk.

name: Daulat ki Chaat
description: Full-cream milk churned overnight into a light foam, topped with khoya, sugar, saffron and dry fruit. It is Old Delhi's version of the North Indian makhan malai and is sold only in the coldest months, roughly late November to early February, because heat melts it.
how_to_eat: Eat it straight away from the leaf or plate with a spoon; it dissolves on the tongue.
how_to_order: Look for vendors with large trays in the lanes of Chandni Chowk on winter mornings; it is sold by the plate.

name: Tandoori Chicken
description: Chicken marinated in yogurt and spices and roasted in a clay tandoor. Punjabi migrants from Peshawar popularised it at Moti Mahal in Daryaganj in the late 1940s, and it became a standard dish at official banquets.
how_to_eat: Eat it with your hands, with sliced onion, lemon and mint chutney.
how_to_order: Ask for a half or full tandoori chicken at tandoor restaurants.
